newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britain sets 5 year London airport pricing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britain sets 5 year London airport pricing.

text.p: Britain's Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) on Thursday ruled that airport operator BAA Plc must cut its airline user charges at London Heathrow and Gatwick by three percentage points below inflation a year for five years.
The CAA added that, within this overall cap, "actual charges at Heathrow will have to rise relative to those at Gatwick by at least 1.0 percent each year".

The CAA's current five-year pricing formula, which governs landing and passenger handling charges at Heathrow, Gatwick and the much smaller London Stansted airport, runs out next April. It said Stansted's new formula would be the inflation measure of the Retail Price Index plus 1.0 percentage point.
The announcement confirmed the proposals first announced by the CAA in July pending further consultations with BAA, airlines and other interested parties.

BAA's first response was to call the measures "challenging" and a welcome end to uncertainty, and it added it believed they could be made to work as it builds up to a planned multi-billion pound investment in Heathrow's fifth terminal.

BAA chief executive Sir John Egan said in a statement, "It will be a real challenge to make the improvements in performance that will be necessary if our capital investment programme of 4.4 billion pounds ($7.0 billion) over the next ten years is to be implemented in full".
The company had said in July it wanted a better deal with the CAA and would be seeking instead to be allowed to increase prices in line with inflation.
However, in its statement on Thursday it said the package would provide "a reliable basis for making decisions to invest in mucch-needed airport capacity".

It would now look to three airport strategies to achieve its aims, which Egan lists as -- minimising the cost of constructing new facilities, maximising rental income by continual innovation, and containing operating costs while providing best levels of service.

The CAA had said in making the proposals it was accepting the main recommendations made in a weighty report by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC), following a six-month investigation it undertook for the CAA under the review process.

The CAA said the formula anticipated Terminal Five investment and was designed to give BAA what the MMC and CAA regard as a fair long term average annual rate of return on capital employed of around 7.5 percent a year over 10 years by proposing RPI minus 3 points for the years 1997-2002 with a view to imposing RPI plus 2 for the subsequent five years to 2007.

The CAA said it would have recommended a tougher formula of RPI minus 8 a year for the five years to 2002 to give a rate of return of 7-1/2 percent but that would have meant a sudden surge in airport charges in the next five years, to take account of new investment, of an average RPI plus 13.5 points.

For the 1997-2002 period the CAA also said on Thursday it would allow BAA to increase the regulated charges "by 70 pence per passenger spread over two years" to compensate for loss of retail revenues if, and when, the European Union abolishes duty-free sales for international travellers within the Union.
It said this was expected to happen in 1999.
BAA's shares, which had risen in early trading ahead of the news, were little affected by the announcement and by 0915 GMT were standing up 11 pence at 516.
